title: Why AI has a weird attention span you must learn to manage · hancrafted
description: AI's attention span, its context window, is a limited resource you have to actively manage: one chat per job, a handoff after real progress or before a break, and for bigger projects one planner chat that hands each step to a fresh chat.

slides.text: Why AI has a weird attention span you must learn to manage A long chat behaves like a long call: its attention is a limited window, so you manage what goes into it. The long phone call You called to settle one thing, and an hour later you hung up. 1 h 22 min , one box a minute: the start, the end and Pepper's cake stay lit. …wait, we never fixed the date.

The long phone call (1/2) Page 1 of 2 The long phone call Called to settle one thing. An hour later you remember the start, the end and one standout, and the one thing you called for is still open. S Sister Call ended · 1:21:40 Let's sort out the holidays! Yes! But first, did you hear about Mum’s new phone? The start stays sharp Primacy effect ( opens in a new tab ) : the first line sets the frame. No, what happened? She sent me forty photos of her thumb. Ha! Did you see the neighbours’ renovation? Don’t get me started. And my back hurts again. The middle blurs Serial-position effect ( opens in a new tab ) : mum’s phone, the renovation, the back: said, not kept. And Pepper ate a whole birthday cake, candles included! The standout survives Von Restorff effect ( opens in a new tab ) : the cake is unlike the rest of the call. Did you try that new recipe? Not yet. Oh, dinner is ready, I have to run. Talk soon, bye! The end stays sharp Recency effect ( opens in a new tab ) : the last minutes are still fresh. …wait, we never fixed the date. The pattern is measured on word lists in the lab; that it holds for an hour-long call is an inference ( )

The long phone call (2/2) Page 2 of 2 AI forgets the middle too A long AI chat has the same shape as the call: the first and the newest messages get used, the middle gets lost, and a detail that keeps coming back survives. Next: invitations. first message of the new chat Fresh chat: invitations Fresh chat 19% used 1 One chat, one job When the topic changes, open a new chat: the hotel question does not carry the catering PDF along. 2 Ask for a handoff, read it, correct it After real progress or before a break: the goal, what is decided, what comes next. The long phone call Recall is U-shaped In free recall of a word list, the first and last items are recalled best and the middle ones worst 1 . Sources (1) Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Why the start sticks People rehearse early items more often than middle ones, and the number of rehearsals predicts recall 1 . Sources (1) Rundus, Analysis of rehearsal processes in free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Why the end sticks Delaying recall with a distractor task removes the recency part but leaves the start intact, which points to two separate stores 1 ; where recency comes from is still debated 2 . Sources (2) Glanzer and Cunitz, Two storage mechanisms in free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Bjork and Whitten, Recency-sensitive retrieval processes in long-term free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org The standout survives An item that differs from its neighbours is remembered better, and it stands out against its context, not on its own 1 2 . Sources (2) von Restorff, Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Hunt, The subtlety of distinctiveness: What von Restorff really did ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Lab lists, not phone calls Every study uses word lists or short material, so that the same pattern holds for an hour-long call is an inference, though the effects are textbook findings 1 . Sources (1) Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

AI forgets the middle too Measured, even for long-input models Relevant information is used best at the beginning or end of the input and worst in the middle, also in models built for long contexts 1 . Sources (1) Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org A built-in pull to the start The first tokens of an input draw strong attention as an "attention sink", even when they carry no meaning 1 . Sources (1) Xiao et al., Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Two position effects Causal masking biases attention toward earlier positions, and relative position encodings favour nearby tokens, which trades off against the accumulating importance of early positions 1 ; that these two together produce the middle dip is an inference, the paper's abstract does not state it. Sources (1) Wu et al., On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The strength varies The dip is strongest when the input fills up to about half the window; beyond that the start advantage fades and the end advantage stays 1 . Sources (1) Veseli et al., Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Planted facts, not chat products The studies plant a fact in the input and test whether the model retrieves it; none tests current chat products, so applying them to a chat is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

The context window The model keeps nothing the Messages API is stateless: it holds no conversation between requests, and the caller passes the earlier user and assistant turns along with the new message 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Messages API reference ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Replies feed back in the model's reply becomes part of the input for the next turn 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Both directions count the context window holds the conversation history plus the newly generated output 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Apps may differ the sources describe the developer API; that a chat app resends the history is an inference, and chat interfaces such as claude.ai can instead manage the window by dropping the oldest content first 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

What happens when the bar fills up Quality falls before the limit on a 13-task benchmark almost all of 17 long-context models lost a lot of accuracy as input grew, and only half kept satisfactory performance at 32K tokens although all claimed 32K or more 1 . Sources (1) Hsieh et al., RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Length alone hurts even with perfect retrieval, performance dropped by 13.9% to 85% as input grew, and the drop persisted when irrelevant tokens were masked out 1 . Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Extra material makes it worse across 18 models, performance degraded with input length in every experiment, and even a single distractor lowered it 1 . Sources (1) Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com What the studies measure the studies measure lost accuracy, not a hallucination mechanism 1 2 . Sources (2) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com Mostly synthetic tests most studies use a planted fact or padded filler and models of 2024 and 2025, and the size of the drop varies by model and task 1 . Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Attention is a budget The attention budget Anthropic describes every token attending to every other, so each added token spreads the same attention thinner; it is a vendor account of the measured drop, not itself measured in the studies 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com The U-shape is measured a model's attention itself shows a U-shape toward the start and end of the input, whether or not those tokens are relevant 1 . Sources (2) Hsieh et al., Found in the Middle: Calibrating Positional Attention Bias Improves Long Context Utilization ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (where the name comes from) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The start is weighted the first few tokens draw strong attention as an attention sink even when they carry no meaning 1 . Sources (1) Xiao et al., Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org No single line where the middle gets too thin differs per model and task; when the needle shares no words with the question, 11 of 13 models advertised at 128K or more fell below half of their short-input score at 32K 1 . Sources (1) Modarressi et al., NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

What we learned so far Two kinds of evidence the human pattern comes from lab word lists 1 , the model pattern from retrieval tests on long inputs 2 ; the match between them is an analogy, not a proof. Sources (2) Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org
What fills the window No speaker notes for this Slide.

What's really in the window Nothing carries over by itself a model holds nothing between requests; memory across chats exists only when an application stores notes outside the model and puts them back into the context 1 . Sources (1) Han, Why does an LLM forget everything between chats? (earlier research file, excludes consumer chat apps) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com Documented for Claude Code its instructions and its saved notes are loaded at the start of every conversation, and Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Loading has a cost longer instruction files consume more context and reduce adherence, and only the first 200 lines or 25KB of the notes index load at the start 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Chat apps document the effect Claude's app saves memory as topics so the next conversation already knows what changed 1 , and Gemini remembers information you share, even in new chats 2 ; that the apps load it at the start is an inference. Sources (2) Anthropic, Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous conversations ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Google, Manage what Gemini remembers about you and customize responses ( opens in a new tab ) support.google.com Not every feature preloads Claude's past-chat search is fetched on request 1 , and ChatGPT looks for relevant context only when it is likely to improve a response 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous conversations ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com OpenAI, Memory in ChatGPT ( opens in a new tab ) help.openai.com

One innocent question Everything is loaded with basic web search every result is loaded into the context window, much of it irrelevant to the request 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Web search tool (Claude API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com It stays search results count as input tokens, in the turn itself and in later turns, and are passed back into later requests, so they remain part of the window 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Web search tool (Claude API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com A PDF is the big bite Anthropic estimates an average web page at about 2,500 tokens and a research-paper PDF at about 125,000 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Web fetch tool (Claude API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com The remedy vendors filter before the window or cap the returned tokens 1 ; OpenAI describes the same shape, with deep research tapping hundreds of sources 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Web fetch tool (Claude API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com OpenAI, Web search (API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com API figures, not app figures these sources describe developer tools; how many pages a given chat app loads per question is not published 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Web search tool (Claude API documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

You can't watch the meter Documented for Claude for users with code execution enabled, Claude summarises earlier messages when a conversation approaches the context limit 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How do usage and length limits work? ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com The only sign the page describes you occasionally seeing Claude "organizing its thoughts", and announces no notice each time; that it hides this on purpose is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How do usage and length limits work? ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com Full history is kept the whole chat is preserved so Claude can reference it after summarising 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How do usage and length limits work? ( opens in a new tab ) support.claude.com A summary can lose things Anthropic warns that over-aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context whose importance only shows later 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Other apps are unknown no vendor page found documents summarising in ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot, and a chat interface may instead drop the oldest content first 1 ; OpenAI's compaction is documented for its API and is opaque 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com OpenAI, Compaction ( opens in a new tab ) developers.openai.com
Managing the attention span No speaker notes for this Slide.

Everyday habits Length itself hurts With perfect retrieval, performance still dropped as input grew, and the drop persisted when irrelevant tokens were replaced by whitespace or masked from attention 1 ; that a fresh, shorter chat avoids the drop is an inference from this, the studies do not test a restart. Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org One job per chat Even a single distractor lowers performance relative to the needle alone, so unrelated material in a chat has a cost 1 . Sources (1) Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com A short recap helped Having the model recite the retrieved evidence before solving, which turns a long task into a short one, improved results 1 ; that a handoff works the same way is an inference. Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

The workflow for bigger projects Clean windows for each part Anthropic's remedy for long tasks includes sub-agents that work with clean windows 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Short tasks beat long ones Turning a long task into a short one improved results, GPT-4o on RULER by up to 4% 1 . Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

script.text: This panel shows the speaker notes and voice script for the Slide you are reading, and follows you as you scroll. Press Alt+N to open or close it.

The long phone call 0:00 – 0:33 A long chat is a long call Imagine the last long phone call you had with someone close, a sister, a friend, your mum. You called to settle one thing, and an hour later you hung up. Before I say a word about AI, I want you to feel what that call left you with, because the question I want to ask you is whether a long AI chat does the same thing to you, so the call comes first and the chat second.

The long phone call 0:00 – 0:18 The start sticks Say you call your sister to sort out the holidays. "Let's sort out the holidays!" is how it starts, and that first line sets the frame for everything after it, so you still remember it at the end. That is called primacy. 0:18 – 0:30 The end sticks You also remember how it ended. "Talk soon, bye", and the last few minutes before it, because they just happened and are still fresh. That is called recency. 0:30 – 0:48 The middle blurs Now the middle. An hour of detail went by, the neighbours' renovation, Mum's new phone, your sister's back pain, and if someone asked you what was in it, you could hardly say. All of it was said, and very little of it stayed. 0:48 – 1:07 One thing stands out Except one thing. Pepper ate a whole birthday cake, candles included. Nobody asked you to keep that, and you can still tell it, because what is different from everything around it survives. That is called the Von Restorff effect, or the isolation effect. 1:07 – 1:26 We never fixed the date And then the punchline. Dinner is ready, she has to run, and you realise: we never fixed the date. The one thing you called for never got settled. (pause) Hold on to that, because the question is whether an AI chat does the same.

AI forgets the middle too 0:00 – 0:26 Meet the summer-party chat So let me introduce a chat that stays with us for the rest of the episode. You plan a company summer party with an AI: 40 people, end of June, a budget of 40,000 euro, and you give it a catering PDF and a guest list. Remember this chat, because we come back to it on every slide that follows. 0:26 – 0:56 It happens in a long chat too Now let it run for an hour. You started with the plan and the budget, and the first messages tend to get used, the latest messages tend to get used, and the middle gets lost. A detail you keep repeating, like the 12 vegetarian guests, survives. Later the budget slips, which is odd for a number from your very first message, and why that happens comes on a later slide. 0:56 – 1:16 A shape, not a brain I'm not saying the AI thinks the way you do. It has no sister and no Mum with a new phone. What I'm saying is that the shape is the same, and a shape is something you can predict, so you know where to expect the slip. 1:16 – 1:32 What a lost detail costs With your sister, a lost detail is funny. With a deadline, it's expensive. So ask yourself which one your chat is: the one with the dog and the cake, or the one with your budget in it.

The AI's attention span 0:00 – 0:17 Why it happens So far you have seen what happens. Now the cause, because once you know how the AI holds a chat, the pattern stops being a surprise, and only after that do we look at what it does to your answers.

The context window 0:00 – 0:18 You type one line You type one short line, say, find three venues in Lisbon. But what the AI receives is the whole conversation so far, from your first message to your last, and it receives all of it with every single message you send. 0:18 – 0:40 There is a size limit That bundle has a maximum size. Picture it as a bar that fills up block by block, one block for every question and every answer, until there is no room left. That bar is the context window. That limit is the AI's attention span: how much it can hold in view at once. 0:40 – 0:48 The term to keep The term to keep is context window. If you remember one word from today, take this one, context window. 0:48 – 1:03 Context engineering There is a name for working with it: context engineering. It means giving the AI the right context at the right time, not the most context, the right one. That is what we manage today.

What happens when the bar fills up 0:00 – 0:34 The start helps, but is no guarantee Now watch what happens as this chat grows. The start still helps, because the first messages tend to be used well, like the opening of the call, but that is no guarantee, and you will see why in a moment. One thing before we go on: the numbers on this slide are illustrative, I picked a 200K window and the little bars that show how much the AI looks at each message, to show the shape, not to measure anything. 0:34 – 0:48 The newest stays sharp The newest stays sharp too. The latest messages are used well, like the last minutes of the call, because they sit right at the end of what the AI is reading. 0:48 – 1:02 The middle blurs The middle blurs. What you said an hour ago sits in the blurry part, and the AI treats it the way you treat the neighbours' renovation: it was there, but it is thin. 1:02 – 1:13 A standout survives And one standout survives. The 12 vegetarian guests, a detail the chat keeps repeating, are still there, and the plan comes back with a vegetarian menu. 1:13 – 1:23 Answers get worse Now something new, and this is where it gets uncomfortable. As the chat fills, the answers get worse. This is called context rot. 1:23 – 1:44 The budget is forgotten Look at the budget. Your very first message said 40,000 euro, and now the plan comes back at 52,300. The start of a chat is attended to well, so it was not lost by its position. It got little attention because it is one short number among many similar ones. 1:44 – 2:06 Filling the gap So here is a small number sitting among all the similar numbers from the offers and the searches, and when the AI can't find it, I think it fills the gap itself with something that sounds plausible. I want to be straight about this: that is my hypothesis, not proven.

Attention is a budget 0:00 – 0:19 A hundred units Think of attention as a budget of a hundred units. And I say it plainly: these numbers, the token counts and the window sizes on this slide are illustrative. I made them up to show the shape, so please don't take them as measurements. 0:19 – 0:37 Where it goes Where does the budget go? A big share to the start, a big share to the newest messages, and what is left is shared out across the middle, thinner and thinner with every message you add. That is why the middle fades. 0:37 – 0:53 A spike in the middle But a detail you keep repeating keeps its share, and it shows as a spike in the middle. The 12 vegetarian guests came up again and again, so they stay bright, while the budget, said once, fades. 0:53 – 1:21 Smart zone and dumb zone Somewhere, the middle gets too thin to trust. Before that line the AI is in the smart zone, beyond it in the dumb zone. Matt Pocock puts the line at 80K tokens on a 200K window and at 150K on a 1M window. That is his number, a rule of thumb, and you only get the zone names now because you have already seen the middle fade. 1:21 – 1:44 Having it is not using it Having it is not the same as using it. Your sister secretly recorded the call, and she still can't find what you said at one hour, 13 minutes and 17 seconds. The recording is complete, and finding one sentence in it is the hard part. A full window works the same way. 1:44 – 2:00 My own line My own line sits at 300K tokens, and only on the 1M window. That is one practitioner's habit, not a law. Yours may differ, and that is fine, as long as it is a line you chose on purpose.

What we learned so far 0:00 – 0:12 Same effects Let's put it together. Long AI conversations show the same effects as long human ones: the start, the end and a standout survive, and the middle blurs. 0:12 – 0:20 The window is the span The reason is that the AI's attention span is its context window, a limited space that fills with every message. 0:20 – 0:37 Manage it So treat it as a resource you manage actively, so that important decisions and information don't get lost in the middle. The rest of the episode is about what goes into that window, and what you do about it.

What fills the window 0:00 – 0:13 More in there than you typed You have seen the window fill with your messages. But your messages are only a part of it, so the next question is what else goes in without you noticing.

What's really in the window 0:00 – 0:13 More than the chat What you see in the chat is only part of what the AI reads. The chat is the visible slice, and around it sit other parts that you never typed. 0:13 – 0:25 Starting instructions First, the starting instructions: text placed in front of your first message, before you type a single word. That way the AI is already briefed before you say anything. 0:25 – 0:43 Memory Second, memory: short notes about you, saved earlier and put back in front of the AI, which is why a new chat already knows a few things about you. It is useful, and it is one more thing in the window. 0:43 – 0:57 The rest The rest are attached files, web pages the AI read, and results from tools and connectors. I only name them today. What matters is that they all share the same window as your chat.

One innocent question 0:00 – 0:13 Three venues Say you ask: find three venues in Lisbon. It is a small question. The answer is three options in a few lines, and behind it the AI ran two searches. 0:13 – 0:24 What you don't see Those searches bring back extracts of web pages that you never see. Each one is a modest bite, and the window takes it and moves on. 0:24 – 0:45 The catering PDF Then you point at the catering offers in the project folder and ask which one fits. The answer is one line, Sabor Verde. To give it, the AI read the whole catering PDF, all twenty pages, and that one question filled the window far more than anything before it. 0:45 – 1:05 The intern Give an intern the same task and they would read the whole file first too, before telling you one line. The AI does exactly that, only fast, and it shows you just the result. There is nothing wrong with it, you only need to know it happened. 1:05 – 1:20 A big bite So one short question can take a big bite out of the window while the chat looks as small as before. Keep that in mind when a chat feels full sooner than you expected.

You can't watch the meter 0:00 – 0:13 Her own notes Your sister doesn't keep the call. She keeps her own notes of it, a few scribbled lines: Mum's phone, the renovation, Pepper and the cake. A few lines instead of everything. 0:13 – 0:27 The app does something like it The app does something like it. When a chat gets long, older messages can be squeezed into a short summary, so the conversation can go on instead of hitting the wall. 0:27 – 0:38 You can't watch the meter And here is the catch: the chat looks the same. Every bubble is still there, so you can't rely on a gauge, you rely on habits. 0:38 – 0:52 Why the budget survived Why did the budget survive here? Because you flagged the 12,300 over budget just before, so it was fresh when the summary was written, and the plan fits 40,000 euro again. That was timing.
Managing the attention span 0:00 – 0:09 You manage by habit You can't read a gauge, so you build habits. First the everyday ones, and then the one for a big project.

Everyday habits 0:00 – 0:11 Break it down Break it down. You know this one already: you split a big task into small steps, and each step is small enough to hold in view. 0:11 – 0:24 Fresh start Fresh start. You know this one too: a fresh start spends the whole window on the work in front of you, and none of it on what happened an hour ago. 0:24 – 0:35 One chat, one job One chat, one job. When the topic changes, open a new chat, so that the hotel question doesn't have to carry the catering PDF along. 0:35 – 0:49 Ask for a handoff Ask for a handoff. After real progress, or before a coffee break, stop and ask the AI for a handoff: a short card with the goal, what is decided and what comes next. 0:49 – 1:02 Read and correct it Then read it and correct what is wrong. A summary can leave things out or get one wrong, and you are the one accountable for what the next chat believes. 1:02 – 1:18 Start the next chat with it And start the next chat with it. Paste the handoff in as the first message, and the new chat starts small and sharp, with the venue, the caterer, the budget and the next step, and nothing else.

The workflow for bigger projects 0:00 – 0:13 One chat is too small Sometimes the project is bigger than one chat can hold: the whole summer party, with venues, catering, hotels and invitations. One chat would fill up, whatever window size you give it. 0:13 – 0:32 Break it down first So you break it down first. Work backward from the outcome, what do I need to run this party, and then what do I need for that, until the next step is clear. You can ask the AI to help you with that. 0:32 – 0:42 One planner Then one chat stays the planner. It keeps only the plan and the results, so it stays small and has room to spare. 0:42 – 1:01 A fresh chat per step Each step goes to a fresh chat: venues, catering, invitations. That chat reads its files and fills up as much as it needs, hands the result back to the planner as one small card, and then you let it go. Next step, next fresh chat. 1:01 – 1:47 You coordinate And you coordinate, like a project manager. This is what we call a workflow. Every chat has one job, so none of them runs long enough to blur its middle. That is the whole idea: the window is the AI's attention span, and managing it is your job. One honest caveat: the zones and numbers I gave you are rules of thumb and illustrations, and I have not tested every chat app, so watch your own chats and adjust. If you want a low-key place to start, take the next chat that drifts, ask it for a handoff, and open a new one with it. Thank you.
